item.title: IoT: Build your perimeter security with Long Range radio
item.content:encoded:
Autonomy technology

Learn how to build your own perimeter security system for a farm or any other remote location using the RPi Pico, ESP32, and long-range radio.

What if you could secure a remote farm, a field, or a property far beyond the reach of Wi-Fi or cellular networks? What if a simple, low-cost system built with microcontrollers could detect an intruder, capture a photo, and alert you over a long-range radio link?

In my previous article, [IoT: How to stay connected when others don’t — with HC-12 radio], I explored how HC-12 radio modules can keep devices connected when conventional networks are unavailable. I also promised to take the idea further. This article delivers on that promise.

Here, we will build an advanced perimeter security system using the Raspberry Pi Pico, ESP32, PIR motion sensors, cameras, and HC-12 radio modules in the EU (or 915 MHz LoRa modules in the US). The system will detect motion, capture photos, and transmit alerts over a long-range wireless link, keeping you informed about security at a remote field, yard, or large forested property.

IoT architecture

The architecture of the solution will consist of different device types. Let’s focus on two main components: Skyfall-client and Guard-host server.

Skyfall-client is a remote sensor node built around an ESP32S3 N16R8 microcontroller, a PIR motion sensor SR501, and an OV2640 camera. When motion is detected, the client captures a photo and transmits the security event and image data over a long-range HC-12 radio link.

Guard-host, built around a Raspberry Pi Pico W and an HC-12 radio module, acts as the central receiver (the server located in the farmhouse). It listens for incoming transmissions from client nodes, processes security events integrating alerts and notifications via a Telegram channel.

Skyfall — PIR Sensor with camera

An advanced perimeter sensor built around the ESP32-S3 microcontroller, combining an HC-SR501 PIR motion sensor with an OV2640 camera. When motion is detected, the node captures a photo and transmits it to the Guard-host via an HC-12 radio module.

Pinout diagram and device configuration for the [Skyfall — PIR Sensor with camera], featuring an onboard 21700 rechargeable battery for standalone operation, see in the corresponding section in the README.md.

main.py

Using an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, PIR motion sensor, OV2640 camera, HC-12 radio module, buzzer, and status LEDs, this file implements basic device logic.

import neopixel

import definitions as vars

from machine import Pin, PWM, ADC, Timer, deepsleep
from radio import RadioHC12
from skyfall import Skyfall
from cam2640 import make_photo
from utime import sleep

# -------------------------
# Configuration
# -------------------------
pir = Pin(vars.PIR_PIN, Pin.IN)
button = Pin(vars.BUTTON_PIN, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
led = neopixel.NeoPixel(Pin(vars.BUTTON_LED_PIN), 1)
ledm = neopixel.NeoPixel(Pin(vars.MUSIC_LED_PIN), 1)
buzzer = PWM(Pin(vars.BUZZER_PIN))
adc = ADC(Pin(vars.ADC_PIN), atten=ADC.ATTN_11DB)

def ledm_on():
    ledm[0] = (0, 0, 255)
    ledm.write()

def ledm_off():
    ledm[0] = (0, 0, 0)
    ledm.write()

def pir_irq(pin):
    global pir_detected
    pir_detected = True

def pir_detection():
    print("Motion detected")
    if secured:
        print("WARNING!!!!")
        play_melody(melody_warning)

        photo_file = 'photo_ov2640.jpg'
        if make_photo(filename=photo_file):
            sleep(1)
            protocol.broadcast_secured_file(
                vars.RADIO_SERVER_ID,
                photo_file)
            
        sleep(2)

def button_irq(pin):
    global btn_clicked
    btn_clicked = True

def button_click():
    global secured
    print("Button pressed")
    secured = not secured

    if secured:
        led[0] = (255, 0, 0)
        print("SECURE ON")
        play_melody(melody_alarm_on)
    else:
        led[0] = (0, 0, 0)
        print("SECURE OFF")
        play_melody(melody_alarm_off)
    led.write()

# -------------------------
# Radio HC-12
# -------------------------
client_radio = RadioHC12(uart_id=vars.RADIO_UART_ID, 
                        tx=vars.RADIO_TX, rx=vars.RADIO_RX, 
                        baudrate=vars.RADIO_BAUDRATE, 
                        my_id=vars.RADIO_MY_ID, 
                        allowed_devices=vars.RADIO_ALLOWED_DEVICES)

protocol = Skyfall(radio_instance=client_radio, 
                   encryption_keys=vars.CLIENT_KEYS)

def protocol_receiver_callback(msg_type, value):
    global secured

    print(f'[RadiO] we have receieved: {msg_type}: {value}')

    if msg_type == Skyfall.MSG_TEXT:
        if 'Arm' in value:
            secured = False
            button_click()
        elif 'Disarm' in value:
            secured = True
            button_click()

# -------------------------
# Buzzer
# -------------------------
melody_start = [
    (523, 0.12),   # C5
    (659, 0.12),   # E5
    (784, 0.16),   # G5
    (1047, 0.35),  # C6
]

melody_alarm_on = [
    (180, 0.30),  # F#3
    (180, 0.15),  # F#3
    (220, 0.25),  # A3
    (180, 0.15),  # F#3
    (330, 0.18),  # E4
    (220, 0.25),  # A3
]

melody_alarm_off = [
    (1760, 0.25),  # A6
    (1320, 0.15),  # E6
    (880, 0.12),   # A5
    (660, 0.40),   # E5
]

melody_warning = [
    (850, 0.50),  # G#5
]

melody_alarm = [
    (1500, 4.0),  # F#6
]

melody_shutdown = [
    (1760, 0.18),  # A6
    (1480, 0.18),  # F#6
    (1320, 0.20),  # E6
    (1100, 0.22),  # C#6
    (880,  0.28),  # A5
    (660,  0.45),  # E5
    (440,  0.65),  # A4
]

def play_tone(freq, duration):
    ledm_on()
    buzzer.freq(freq)
    buzzer.duty_u16(vars.BUZZER_VOLUME)
    sleep(duration)
    buzzer.duty_u16(0)
    ledm_off()
    sleep(0.03)

def play_melody(melody):
    buzzer.init()
    for note, duration in melody:
        play_tone(note, duration)
    buzzer.deinit()
    ledm_off()

# -------------------------
# Battery
# -------------------------
def battery_check(timer):
    global need_shutdown

    divider_ratio = (470 + 100) / 100 #5.7

    raw = adc.read_u16()
    voltage = raw * 3.4 * divider_ratio / 65535

    print(f"RAW: {raw:5d}  VSYS: {voltage:.2f} V")

    if voltage < vars.LOW_BATTERY:
        print("Low battery")
        need_shutdown = True

# -------------------------
# Shutdown
# -------------------------
def shutdown():
    print('>shutdown!')

    pir.irq(handler=None)
    button.irq(handler=None)
    led[0] = (0, 0, 0)
    led.write()

    timer.deinit()
    timer = None
    
    play_melody(melody_shutdown)
    ledm_on()
    sleep(2)
    ledm_off()
    sleep(1)
    deepsleep()

# -------------------------
# Init
# -------------------------
secured = False
btn_clicked = False
pir_detected = False
need_shutdown = False

pir.irq(trigger=Pin.IRQ_RISING,
        handler=pir_irq)

button.irq(trigger=Pin.IRQ_FALLING,
        handler=button_irq)

timer = Timer(0)
timer.init(
    period=1 * 60 * 1000, # 60 sec
    mode=Timer.PERIODIC,
    callback=battery_check)

# -------------------------
# Main loop
# -------------------------
play_melody(melody_start)

while True:
    print('...')
    if pir_detected:
        sleep(0.5)
        pir_detection()
        pir_detected = False
    if btn_clicked:
        sleep(0.5)
        button_click()
        btn_clicked = False
    if need_shutdown:
        shutdown()

    try:
        if client_radio.uart.any() != 0:
            protocol.read_secured_packages(
                    on_message=protocol_receiver_callback,
                    uart_timeout=vars.RADIO_UART_TIMEOUT_MS)
    except: pass

    sleep(0.5)

This micro-python code above implements the perimeter security sensor (Skyfall-client) logic:

  • Motion detection: The PIR sensor triggers an interrupt. When security mode is enabled, the device sounds a warning, captures a photo, and transmits it securely to the Guard-host server via the HC-12 radio link.
  • Security control: A physical button toggles security mode on and off, with LED indicators and audio feedback.
  • Radio communication: Receives remote arm/disarm commands from the Guard-host and broadcasts encrypted security events and photos.
  • Battery monitoring: Checks the battery voltage every 60 seconds and initiates shutdown when it falls below the configured threshold (3.5V).
  • Power management: Plays a shutdown melody, disables interrupts, and enters deep sleep when the battery is low (less then 3.5V).
  • Audio feedback: Uses a PWM buzzer and an LED to indicate startup, security mode changes, warnings, and shutdown.

cam2640.py

This file initializes the OV2640 camera using the micro-python Camera API, configures JPEG capture at CIF resolution, and provides a make_photo() function to capture an image and save it to a file.

from camera import Camera, GrabMode, PixelFormat, FrameSize

cam = None

try:
    cam = Camera(
                data_pins=[16,17,18,8,9,10,11,12],
                vsync_pin=6,
                href_pin=7,
                sda_pin=4,
                scl_pin=5,
                pclk_pin=13,

                xclk_pin=-1,
                powerdown_pin=-1,
                reset_pin=-1,

                pixel_format=PixelFormat.JPEG,
                frame_size=FrameSize.CIF,
                jpeg_quality=90,
                fb_count=2,
                grab_mode=GrabMode.LATEST)

    print("[CAMERA] initialization is OK")

except Exception as e:
    print("[CAMERA] initialization ERROR:", repr(e))

def make_photo(filename=''):

    if filename == '' or cam is None:
        return False

    try:
        img = bytes(cam.capture()) 

        with open(filename, "wb") as f:
            f.write(img)

        cam.free_buffer()
        f.close()
        return True
    
    except:
        return False

File above handles initialization and capture errors by returning a failure status in case of exception.

The Skyfall-client device also uses two supporting modules, skyfall.py and radio.py, which handle the security protocol, encrypted message exchange, and HC-12 radio communication, as described earlier in the related article - Skyfall radio protocol.

Firmware for Skyfall-client

The Skyfall-client also has an install.md file in the appropriate repository. The main challenge is to flash the ESP32-S3 with compatible firmware that supports the OV2640 camera.

Guard-host — Radio receiver/server

The central server of the system is built around the Raspberry Pi Pico W (RP2040 W). It receives motion events and photos from all sensor nodes via HC-12 radio, connects to the farmhouse Wi-Fi network via ESP8285 module, and forwards security alerts to Telegram. It also supports remote arming and disarming of all nodes of the perimeter security system.

Pinout diagram and device configuration for [Guard-host — Radio receiver in the farmhouse], powered via a 5V USB cable for standalone operation, see in the corresponding section in the README.md.

main.py

This file implements the core logic for the Guard-host device. It receives security events and photos from Skyfall-client nodes, forwards alerts and images to Telegram, and supports remote arming and disarming of the perimeter security system via Telegram commands. It also handles Wi-Fi reconnection, queues incoming radio messages for Telegram delivery, and uses LED signals to indicate system status and communication activity.

import os
import utime

import definitions as vars

from utime import sleep
from machine import Pin
from wifi import WiFi
from radio import RadioHC12
from skyfall import Skyfall
from telega import Telegram

# -------------------------
# Configuration
# -------------------------
led = Pin(vars.NETWORK_LED_PIN, Pin.OUT)

# -------------------------
# WiFi
# -------------------------
wifi_client = WiFi(uart_id=vars.WIFI_UART_ID, 
                   baudrate=vars.WIFI_UART_BAUDRATE)

# -------------------------
# Telega
# -------------------------
telegram_client = Telegram(wifi_client=wifi_client,
                  telegram_host=vars.TELEGRAM_HOST,
                  telegram_bot_id=vars.TELEGRAM_BOT_ID,
                  telegram_chat_id=vars.TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID)

# -------------------------
# Radio HC-12
# -------------------------
server_radio = RadioHC12(uart_id=vars.RADIO_UART_ID, 
                        tx=vars.RADIO_TX, 
                        rx=vars.RADIO_RX, 
                        baudrate=vars.RADIO_BAUDRATE, 
                        my_id=vars.RADIO_MY_ID, 
                        allowed_devices=vars.RADIO_ALLOWED_DEVICES)

protocol = Skyfall(radio_instance=server_radio, 
                   encryption_keys=vars.SERVER_KEYS)

def protocol_receiver_callback(msg_type, value):
    print(f'[RadiO] we have receieved: {msg_type}: {value}')
    telegram_queue.append((msg_type, value))

# -------------------------
# Light signals
# -------------------------
signal_init = [
    (1, 0.15), (0, 0.15),
    (1, 0.15), (0, 0.15),
    (1, 0.15), (0, 0.15),
    (1, 3), (0, 0.21)
]

signal_wifi_connect = [
    (1, 0.7), (0, 0.2),
    (1, 0.18), (0, 0.2),
    (1, 0.18)
]

signal_wifi_reconect = [
    (1, 0.5), (0, 0.5),
    (1, 0.5), (0, 0.5),
    (1, 0.5), (0, 0.5),
    (1, 0.5), (0, 0.5),
    (1, 0.5), (0, 0.5),
]

signal_start_sending = [
    (1, 0.18), (0, 0.7), (1, 0.5)
]

signal_end_sending = [
    (0, 0.21), (1, 0.4), (0, 0.23), 
    (1, 0.18), (0, 0.21)
]

signal_reply_start_sending = [
    (1, 1), (0, 0.4), (1, 0.6)
]

signal_reply_end_sending = [
    (0, 0.21), (1, 1), (0, 0.4),
    (1, 0.6), (0, 0.21)
]

def light_led(value, duration):
    led.value(value)
    sleep(duration)
    sleep(0.03)

def light_signal(signal):
    for value, duration in signal:
        light_led(value, duration)

# -------------------------
# Init
# -------------------------
light_signal(signal_init)

light_signal(signal_wifi_connect)
wifi_client.connect(hostname=vars.WIFI_CLIENT_HOSTNAME, 
                    network=vars.WIFI_NETWORK_NAME, 
                    password=vars.WIFI_NETWORK_PASSWORD)
led.off()

# -------------------------
# Main loop
# -------------------------
offset = 0
telegram_queue = []
telegram_last_time = (utime.ticks_ms() - 
                      vars.TELEGRAM_UPDATES_TIMEOUT_MS)

while True:
    print('...')
    led.off()

    try:
        # --- RADIO HC-12 UART LISTENING ---
        last_uart_time = utime.ticks_ms()
        while (utime.ticks_diff(
            utime.ticks_ms(), last_uart_time) <= vars.RADIO_UART_TIMEOUT_MS):
            try:
                if server_radio.uart.any() != 0:
                    protocol.read_secured_packages(file_prefix='radio_file_',
                                                file_ext='jpg',
                                                on_message=protocol_receiver_callback,
                                                uart_timeout=vars.RADIO_UART_TIMEOUT_MS)
                    last_uart_time = utime.ticks_ms()
            except: pass
            utime.sleep_ms(5)

        # --- END RADIO HC-12 UART LISTENING ---

        # --- TELEGRAM & NETWORK EXECUTION ---
        if utime.ticks_diff(
            utime.ticks_ms(), telegram_last_time) >= vars.TELEGRAM_UPDATES_TIMEOUT_MS:
            if wifi_client.reconnect(vars.WIFI_NETWORK_NAME, 
                                vars.WIFI_NETWORK_PASSWORD):           
                
                telegram_last_time = utime.ticks_ms()

                # Getting updates from Telegram and reaction
                try:
                    light_signal(signal_start_sending)
                    res = telegram_client.get_updates(offset=offset)
                    light_signal(signal_end_sending)
                    if res is not None:
                        sender_id, update_id, text = res
                        offset = update_id + 1
                        reply_text = ''
                        if str(sender_id) == vars.TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID:
                            if text == 'Arm':
                                reply_text = f'Arming ...'
                            elif text == 'Disarm':
                                reply_text = f'Disarming ...'
                            else:
                                reply_text = f'Unknown command {text}'
                        else:
                            reply_text = f'Not authorized sender {sender_id} on update {update_id}'

                        if reply_text != '':
                            light_signal(signal_reply_start_sending)
                            telegram_client.send_message(reply_text)
                            light_signal(signal_reply_end_sending)

                        if text == 'Arm' or text == 'Disarm':
                            for dst_id, key in vars.SERVER_KEYS.items():
                                light_signal(signal_reply_start_sending)
                                protocol.broadcast_secured_message(dst_id, text)
                                sleep(0.4)
                                light_signal(signal_reply_end_sending)
                except: pass

                # Executing queue 
                while len(telegram_queue) > 0:
                    try:
                        msg_type, msg_val = telegram_queue.pop(0)

                        led.on()
                        if msg_type == Skyfall.MSG_FILE:
                            telegram_client.send_photo(
                                            msg_val, 
                                            f'[File: {msg_val}]')
                            sleep(1)
                            if msg_val in os.listdir(): 
                                os.remove(msg_val)
                        elif msg_type == Skyfall.MSG_TEXT:
                            telegram_client.send_message(msg_val)
                        led.off()
                        sleep(0.1)
                    except RuntimeError as que:
                        print(f'{que}')
            else:
                # if no connection - error
                light_signal(signal_wifi_reconect)
        # --- END TELEGRAM & NETWORK EXECUTION ---
    except RuntimeError as ex:
        print(ex)

This micro-python code and its main loop implement the perimeter security server (Guard-host) main logic:

  • HC-12 radio reception: Listens for incoming security events, text messages, and photos from sensor nodes using the Skyfall protocol.
  • Wi-Fi connection management: Reconnects to the configured Wi-Fi network when necessary.
  • Telegram command handling: Retrieves Telegram updates and processes Arm and Disarm commands.
  • Remote security control: Broadcasts arming and disarming commands to configured sensor nodes (Skyfall-client, Thunderball-client) using the secure radio protocol.
  • Telegram notifications: Sends received text alerts and captured photos to the configured Telegram chat.
  • File management: Deletes transmitted photo files after sending them to Telegram chanel.
  • Status indication: Uses LED patterns to indicate initialization, Wi-Fi connectivity, and message transmission activity.

other receiver files

  • wifi.py — Provides a wrapper for the ESP8285 Wi-Fi module, enabling Wi-Fi connectivity.
  • telega.py — Uses the Wi-Fi module and its TLS/SSL connection to communicate with the Telegram Bot API, sending text messages and photo files to the configured Telegram chat.
  • skyfall.py — Implements the Skyfall secure communication protocol.
  • radio.py — Handles HC-12 radio communication used by the Skyfall protocol for secure data exchange between devices.

Firmware for Guard-host

The Guard-host radio receiver/server requires a more complex firmware configuration because it uses an ESP8285 module. To update its firmware properly and ensure support for SSL/TLS, which is required for Telegram communication, you need to follow the instructions in theinstall.md file from an appropriate repository.

MicroFence — perimeter security system on microcontrollers

Both devices described above are part of the MicroFence perimeter security project. Each device has its own configuration settings in definitions.py, covering Wi-Fi credentials, radio communication parameters, and Telegram integration variables. Follow the setup instructions in the project's README.md and configure each device according to its specific requirements.

Besides these two devices, MicroFence includes another device type: the Thunderball-client. It works similarly to the Skyfall-client but does not include a camera. Since its functionality is largely the same, I won’t cover it in detail in this article.

MicroFence is a perimeter security system built around Raspberry Pi Pico and ESP32 microcontrollers. It combines hardware-based motion detection, photo capture, and long-range HC-12 wireless communication (up to 1–2 km) to deliver real-time intrusion detection, reliable alerts to the farmhouse, and instant Telegram notifications over farmhouse Wi-Fi network.

MicroFence is an evolving open-source project, with more features and device types planned for the future. Upcoming developments include Google Gemini integration for on-the-fly image recognition (animal, person, etc) and Home Assistant MQTT integration.

Stay tuned for what’s next!

micro files

The source code for all device types described in this article can be downloaded and freely reused from the GitHub repository. All code is released under the MIT license.

item.title: How much should you fine-tune your vision transformer with limited data
item.content:encoded:
In this experiment I wanted to understand how much of my Vision Transformer (ViT) should I fine tune to my limited dataset for a better performance. Figures were created with AI assistance from the recorded experimental results.

In production environments we always run into scenarios were there is not enough data or if there is it has limited labels and annotations. I wanted to understand which model can perform better on a sample limited dataset representing this case. And how much of the model do I need to fine tune in order for it to adapt to this dataset.

Why I started with a classifier

Classification is a good benchmark for testing assumptions and ideas. Additionally, it is a good probe for comparing the performance of different models even though the down stream application might be something different.

That is why I started with a subset of the Food-101. I extracted 5000 images from the dataset containing 20 classes of different foods. The dataset was straitifed into 4000 training and 1000 validation images. The validation data was the benchmark for comparing all model performances.

Selecting the contenders

It is hard to separate a weak architecture from a poorly trained model due to limited data and compute resources. These are why I used pretrained models to only fine tune and adapt to the dataset instead of training them from scratch.

So my selected contenders were ResNet50 to use as a global benchmark due to its established performance and familiar convolution reference point, ConvNeXt-Tiny as a modern CNN based model that has adapted to the architecture of transformers, a small ViT , DeiT-Tiny, representing the transformers. Using smaller models is more suitable for my small dataset and makes the fine tuning question more tractable: When can I get a meaningful adaptation of my model to my dataset?

Seven ways to ask the same question

I tested 5 different variants of the DeiT-Tiny model and fully fine tuned ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny model. Each model was run for 10 epochs. The data was preprocessed according to each models requirement and the hyperparameters also differed based on the training strategy.

I fine tuned DeiT-Tiny with different strategies:

  • classifier head only
  • LORA adapters
  • fine tuning the last three transformer blocks
  • fine tuning the last five transformer blocks
  • fine tuning the full model

I also fine-tuned ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny to give me a benchmark against the CNN family models.

As shown in the figure below the DeiT-last 5 achieved the highest performance amongst the DeiT variations with 83.3% validation accuracy. The interesting part of the experiment was the performance of the ConvNeXt-Tiny which substantailly outperformed the DeiT variations and ResNet-50 models achieving 87.9% validation accuracy.

DeiT-last 3 reached 81.6% while DeiT-head achieved 74.0% and DeiT-LoRA arrived at 75.4% validation accuracy. Another important parameter to take into account considering the limited compute resources is the number of paramters trained for each model. DeiT- last 5 trained about 2.23 million parameters whereas DeiT-LoRA only trained 0.08 million. DeiT-LoRA reached 75.4% accuracy while training about 0.08 million parameters, roughly 28 times fewer than DeiT-last 5. That saved trainable parameters at a cost of 7.9 percentage points of validation accuracy. ResNet-50 reached 70.3%.

Is training more layer really better?

With fine tuning and updating all the layers and parameters of a model, we introduce many more decisions for the optimizer. This can be averted by limiting it to only a few final layers specifically on smaller datasets. This forces the model to adapt only the higher level features and preserve the useful virtual structure of the image. This can give the models room to adjust to new categories.

Using more advanced techniques like LoRA had its benefits with the reduced number of parameters but that came with the trade-off of lower accuracy score. That is a practical evidence on the compromise between efficiency and performance.

The CNN comparison changed the question again

CNN family has been a go to when it comes to processing images with the localized convolution layers where they can extract very useful features. However, not always we care about locality in the images. Some applications need the global relationship between features from different parts of the image and this is where a transformer based architecture shines.

In this experiment, ResNet-50 lagged behind the DeiT varaints even though it was a classification task which is the specialty of CNNs. However, with ConvNeXt-Tiny dominated the experiment by achieving 87.9% validation score, it shows me that even though transformer models performed better at classifying an image, the hybrid structure is more adaptable to the constraints of this experiment.

Was ConvNeXt really the best model for this application?

Using one metric to compare models performances is not the best practice. A top-1 accuracy score only tells us how often the model had the right answer. It does not tell us anything about the confidence of the model or if the correct class was in the top-3 or top-5 options if misclassified.

In order to gain a better understanding of the models’ true behaviour I also checked the confusion matrix, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, confidence score, calibration error and margin between top two predicted classes.

Confusion matrix shows which categories were mixed up, while the top-5 accuracy tells me how often the correct answer was in the top-5 choices of the model. Macro F1 averages each class’s F1 score equally. I used the per-class scores and confusion matrix to see which food classes were performing poorly.

Expected Calibration Error (ECE) was one of the most important metrics to me because it tells me how much of the model’s prediciton matches its confidence score. In this run, the expected calibration error was about 0.035 for DeiT-last 5 model, 0.064 for ConvNeXt-Tiny, and 0.277 for ResNet-50 (lower is better).

It is apparent that the ResNet-50 has the highest ECE score while its top-1 mean confidence is only 42.6% which suggests how underconfident it is. More interestingly, ConvNeXt-Tiny despite having the highest validation accuracy has a higher ECE than the DeiT-last 5 which suggest that the highest accuracy model is not the best calibrated.

Figure above shows the top-1 and top-5 accuracy of each model. It is interesting to note that the gap in the top-1 accuracy between each model is quite substantial compared to the top-5 accuracy. Even though the models performed differently when they only needed to output one class, the correct class was mostly in their top-5 answers. This is yet another evidence that relying only on a single accuracy score will not determine the best model.

The top 2 probability margin also illustrates the confidence of the ConvNeXt-Tiny and DeiT-last 5 models. They are the two models that had the most confidence in their answers although this does not necessarily guarantee they were always correct. Combined with accuracy scores and ECE, this present a more concrete evidence as to why these two models had the highest accuracy.

Conclusion and future work

Model selection, number of layers to fine tune are highly dependant on the amount of data, compute power available to you and the end task the model is used for. On this dataset and training recipe, DeiT-last 5 performed better than DeiT-full and full fine tuned ConvNeXt-Tiny achieved the highest accuracy.

The lesson I take from this is that how much of a pretrained model to fine-tune is a choice worth testing. Making more layers trainable did not automatically improve the result.

That leaves me with two questions:

1- what happens if I fine tune the ConvNeXt partially similar to the DeiT-Tiny model?

2- Is ConvNeXt going to perform better than a VLM as well?

Have you seen partial fine-tuning beat full fine-tuning on a small dataset? I would be interested to hear what changed when you adjusted the data or training recipe.

item.title: Building a Distributed Job Throttler: Combining SQS Delayed Queues and Redis Atomic Locks
item.content:encoded:
Handling bursty webhook storms and heavy AI background workloads without queue flooding

It is a familiar backend headache: an external platform (such as GitHub push events, Stripe payment updates, Shopify order webhooks, or CRM integrations) suddenly fires dozens of webhook events in rapid succession for the same entity (repo_id, order_id, customer_id). Because these events originate from third-party systems, client-side debouncing in the browser is completely off the table.

For simple database row updates, absorbing these bursts is trivial. But the moment each incoming webhook triggers an expensive downstream background job — such as multi-minute LLM document analysis, full-repository AI code reviews, or vector embedding re-indexing — the equation changes completely.

Firing an expensive AI background task (costing 0.10–0.10–0.50+ and taking minutes of compute) for every single webhook arriving within seconds will instantly blow up cloud bills and trigger downstream provider rate limits (HTTP 429). The business demand is clear and pragmatic: “While webhooks are storming in for the same entity, hold off on the heavy background job. Once the incoming events stay quiet for a minute, run the AI pipeline just once with the latest state.”

From an engineering perspective, this translates directly to server-side debouncing and throttling background jobs sharing the same business key within a rolling time window.

When approaching this problem, many engineers first consider building a scheduling queue with Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET). However, in production, Redis is an in-memory, volatile storage engine. Node failovers, memory evictions, or transient crashes can permanently wipe scheduled business jobs without a trace.

For mission-critical workloads, our foundational architectural principle was clear: Amazon SQS must serve as the durable message backbone for persistence and at-least-once delivery, while Redis operates strictly as a fast first line of defense (coordinating cache) for rapid state inspection and cooldown flags.

This article details how we designed a hybrid serverless job throttler that strictly separates SQS durability from Redis caching, tackling a plug-and-play abstraction supporting any LLM workload with a single job_name, atomic first-run coordination, dual-bucket batch deduplication, and the calculated financial ROI of synchronous middleman Lambda billing.

1. Overall Architecture and Separation of Concerns

The architectural division of responsibility is simple:

  • 🛡️ SQS (Durable Backbone / Message Queue): Retains raw messages safely for up to 14 days and guarantees at-least-once delivery. Even if Redis crashes completely, business messages are never lost.
  • ⚡ Redis (First Line of Defense / Fast Coordination): Manages fast timestamps for throttle window calculations and cooldown flags to suppress duplicate enqueueing. Fails open on outages.

“With Idempotency Keys Already in Place, Why Use Both Redis and MQ?”

Senior engineers immediately ask: “If the downstream service already enforces idempotency via an idempotency_key, why not just push everything directly to SQS and process asynchronously? Why introduce Redis and complicate the infrastructure?"

  • ❌ The SQS-Only Pitfall (Queue Flooding & Lambda Concurrency Starvation):
    When external webhooks burst or upstream systems fire rapid event cascades, routing every event directly to SQS floods the queue with thousands of duplicate messages. Even if the downstream handler processes them idempotently, waking up hundreds of concurrent Lambda containers to burn compute on redundant messages drains the AWS account concurrency pool and spikes infrastructure costs.
  • ❌ The Redis-Only Pitfall (Missing Durability & No Serverless Timer):
    Redis in-memory queues (ZSET) permanently drop business payloads during node restarts or evictions. Furthermore, executing a “run 60 seconds from now” debounce requires a 24/7 background polling daemon (an EC2 instance running ZRANGEBYSCORE), destroying the serverless, zero-maintenance architecture.
  • ✅ The Resolution: Clear Division of Responsibility
    ➔ Redis (Buffer Shield): Does not guarantee business correctness; it serves as a Buffer Shield in front of the queue, collapsing duplicate bursts to protect SQS from queue flooding and concurrency exhaustion.
    ➔ SQS (Durable Queue & Delay Engine): Provides 14-day message durability and acts as an autonomous Serverless Timer (Delay Engine), waking up Lambda at zero idle cost after the debounce window expires.

The end-to-end processing topology is structured as follows:

2. Plug-and-Play Abstraction: Mapping job_name to Execute Any LLM Job

The greatest operational advantage of this architecture is that it is not tightly coupled to any specific business domain (such as translation or scoring) — it functions as a generic asynchronous job execution engine.

Whenever a team needs to introduce a new, time-consuming, or high-cost LLM/AI task, they never need to provision new queuing infrastructure or write custom throttling logic:

1) Convention-Based Dynamic Dispatching

The Worker Lambda dynamically inspects the message's job_name to determine the target Lambda function:

# worker/lambda_function.py
# Default naming convention: {STAGE}-tj-{job_name}-worker
worker_function_name = f"{STAGE}-tj-{job_name}-worker"
if job_name in JOB_WORKERS:
    worker_function_name = JOB_WORKERS[job_name]

2) Four Shared Enterprise Capabilities for Any LLM Workload Out of the Box

Clients simply send a POST /throttle_job request specifying job_name, idempotency_key, and latency: 60, immediately unlocking:

  • 1️⃣ Deduplication (Debounce / Throttle): Even if triggered dozens of times within 60 seconds, it executes exactly once
  • 2️⃣ Automated Exponential Backoff Retries: Failed jobs automatically retry up to 5 times at 1-minute, 2-minute, and 3-minute intervals
  • 3️⃣ Slack Observability & Alerting: On 5 consecutive failures, the stack automatically sends full error traces and execution duration to a Slack channel
  • 4️⃣ Pipeline Chaining: Downstream steps (next_jobs) passed as an array run sequentially upon completion
💡 Handling Large Payloads Beyond SQS 256KB (Claim-Check Pattern)
Amazon SQS enforces a strict 256KB message limit. For AI workloads processing long-form documents or large scoring inputs that exceed this ceiling, clients apply the standard Claim-Check pattern — persisting the raw payload in S3 and passing an s3_payload_url pointer in the message.

As engineering teams continually roll out new AI features across the organization — such as translation (translate), text categorization (tagging), or applicant evaluation (scoring)—simply mapping the function name grants full distributed idempotency and throttling instantly.

3. Entry Point: Atomic Lua Scripts for First-Run Claiming and Permanent Lock Prevention

At the Entry Point layer, a practical implementation detail is managing first-run claiming and lock safety when multiple concurrent requests arrive with the same key.

If the Entry Point merely inspects Redis (GET) and leaves state creation to the downstream worker, multiple requests arriving within the same millisecond would all see started_at = None. Every concurrent execution would assume it was first, routing duplicate messages straight into the immediate Worker Queue.

The Non-Atomic Pitfall (HSETNX + EXPIRE), Permanent Locks, and Cycle Resets

Initially, one might attempt calling hsetnx and subsequently invoking expire in Python application code. In a distributed serverless runtime, this harbors a catastrophic bug:
If the Lambda container is terminated by an OOM error or encounters a network socket timeout immediately after hsetnx, the key is left with TTL = -1 (Infinite persistence). The idempotency key is permanently locked, and subsequent requests will never reset their throttle window.

Furthermore, once the debounce window (latency) expires, subsequent user actions on the same key must atomically reset the window and claim a fresh execution cycle (diff <= 0).

To solve this, we execute an atomic Lua script that bundles first-run claiming, debounce window evaluation, cycle reset, and TTL configuration into a single transaction — coupled with an Entry Point Fail-Open fallback:

# lambda/shared_redis/redis_utils.py & entry-point/lambda_function.py
EVALUATE_AND_CLAIM_LUA = """
local started_epoch = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'started_epoch')
local now_epoch = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local latency = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local ttl = tonumber(ARGV[4])
if not started_epoch then
    -- Claim first execution
    redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'started_at', ARGV[1], 'started_epoch', ARGV[2], 'status', 'running')
    redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ttl)
    return {1, 0}
else
    local diff = (tonumber(started_epoch) + latency) - now_epoch
    if diff <= 0 then
        -- Previous window expired -> Atomically reset and claim a fresh cycle!
        redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'started_at', ARGV[1], 'started_epoch', ARGV[2], 'status', 'running')
        redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ttl)
        return {1, 0}
    else
        -- Throttle window still active -> Return remaining delay
        return {0, diff}
    end
end
"""
key = get_job_key(job_name, idempotency_key)
now_epoch = int(now.timestamp())
try:
    # ⚡ Atomically evaluate window and claim execution or retrieve remaining delay
    result = redis_client.eval(EVALUATE_AND_CLAIM_LUA, 1, key, now.isoformat(), now_epoch, latency, 24 * 60 * 60)
    is_first, remaining_delay = result[0], result[1]
except Exception as redis_err:
    # 🛡️ Entry Point Fail-Open: Forward immediately to worker queue on cache downtime
    logger.warning(f"Redis unavailable: {redis_err}. Failing open to worker queue.")
    send_to_worker_queue(job_data)
    return {'statusCode': 200, 'message': 'Job queued to worker queue (fail-open)'}
if is_first == 1:
    try:
        # Exactly one winner claims the execution and routes immediately to Worker Queue
        send_to_worker_queue(job_data)
        return {'statusCode': 200, 'message': 'Job queued to worker queue'}
    except Exception as sqs_err:
        # 💥 Delete the claimed Redis key on SQS enqueue failure (compensating transaction rollback)
        redis_client.delete(key)
        raise
else:
    # Active-window requests are isolated into Main Queue with exact remaining delay (capped at 900s)
    delay_seconds = min(max(int(remaining_delay), 1), 900)
    send_to_main_queue_with_delay(job_data, delay_seconds)
    return {'statusCode': 200, 'message': 'Job throttled to main queue'}
💡 AWS SQS 15-Minute (900s) Ceiling Guardrail
Amazon SQS DelaySeconds has a hard cloud limit of 900 seconds (15 minutes). For debounce windows exceeding 15 minutes, the system caps the delay at min(delay_seconds, 900) and re-enqueues in 15-minute hops, or delegates long-duration delays to AWS Step Functions / EventBridge Scheduler.

4. Consumer: Intra-Batch Deduplication and Dual-Bucket Routing

When SQS messages in the Main Queue reach visibility after their delay expires, SQS delivers them to the MainQueueConsumer Lambda in batches of up to 10 records.

Here, two critical challenges arise:

  1. Intra-Batch Duplicate Storms: If multiple messages for the same key entered the Main Queue during the throttle window, they emerge together in the same batch. Evaluating them independently causes duplicate messages to be forwarded to the Worker Queue or re-enqueued simultaneously.
  2. Coexisting Disparate Schedules: If a single batch contains both a message whose delay has expired (delay <= 0, ready for immediate execution) and a newly arrived message requiring future delay (delay = 60), naive single-item deduplication would silently drop one of the valid schedules.

To resolve this, we partition records into ready_jobs and delayed_jobs buckets and report granular partial batch failures (batchItemFailures) paired with release_dedup_lock:

# lambda/main-queue-consumer/lambda_function.py
ready_jobs = {}    # Jobs ready for Worker Queue immediately
delayed_jobs = {}  # Jobs requiring re-enqueuing into Main Queue with delay
batch_item_failures = []
for record in records:
    mid = record.get('messageId')
    try:
        # ... Query started_at from Redis and compute delay_seconds against settings
        if delay_seconds <= 0:
            if group_key not in ready_jobs:
                ready_jobs[group_key] = {'job_data': job_data, 'invoked_at': invoked_at, 'message_ids': [mid]}
            else:
                ready_jobs[group_key]['message_ids'].append(mid)
                if invoked_at >= ready_jobs[group_key]['invoked_at']:
                    ready_jobs[group_key]['job_data'] = job_data
                    ready_jobs[group_key]['invoked_at'] = invoked_at
        else:
            # Retain only the latest payload for jobs still requiring delay
            if group_key not in delayed_jobs:
                delayed_jobs[group_key] = {
                    'job_data': job_data, 'invoked_at': invoked_at, 
                    'delay_seconds': min(delay_seconds, 900),
                    'message_ids': [mid]
                }
            else:
                delayed_jobs[group_key]['message_ids'].append(mid)
                if invoked_at >= delayed_jobs[group_key]['invoked_at']:
                    delayed_jobs[group_key]['job_data'] = job_data
                    delayed_jobs[group_key]['invoked_at'] = invoked_at
    except Exception as e:
        batch_item_failures.append({"itemIdentifier": mid})
# 1. Forward ready jobs (lock:ready:{group_key})
for group_key, item in ready_jobs.items():
    ready_lock = f"lock:ready:{group_key}"
    if acquire_dedup_lock(redis_client, ready_lock, ttl=10):
        try:
            send_to_worker_queue(item['job_data'])
        except Exception as e:
            release_dedup_lock(redis_client, ready_lock)  # 🔓 Release lock
            for mid in item.get('message_ids', []):
                batch_item_failures.append({"itemIdentifier": mid})  # 🔁 SQS retries only this item
# 2. Re-enqueue delayed jobs (lock:delayed:{group_key})
for group_key, item in delayed_jobs.items():
    delay_lock = f"lock:delayed:{group_key}"
    # Capped at 30s (strictly below SQS 300s Visibility Timeout to prevent drop on redelivery)
    if acquire_dedup_lock(redis_client, delay_lock, ttl=min(max(item['delay_seconds'], 5), 30)):
        try:
            send_to_main_queue_with_delay(item['job_data'], item['delay_seconds'])
        except Exception as e:
            release_dedup_lock(redis_client, delay_lock)  # 🔓 Release lock
            for mid in item.get('message_ids', []):
                batch_item_failures.append({"itemIdentifier": mid})  # 🔁 SQS retries only this item
# Successful records are deleted (ACKed) by SQS; only failed messageIds are retried
return {'batchItemFailures': batch_item_failures}

No matter how many duplicate records arrive in a single batch, the consumer compresses them into the single latest payload per key and safely ACKs processed records via SQS partial failure reporting (batchItemFailures).

5. Multi-Instance Cooldown Guards & Fail-Open Resilience

When batches are split across multiple concurrent Lambda containers, instances check TTL-based cooldown keys (SET NX EX) in Redis immediately before enqueuing:

  • Worker Queue Routing: Only the instance holding lock:ready:{group_key} (TTL 10s) enqueues to Worker Queue.
  • Main Queue Re-enqueuing: Only the instance holding lock:delayed:{group_key} (TTL: capped at 30s) re-enqueues to Main Queue.

The Fail-Open Principle: Zero Message Loss During Cache Outages

Crucially, Redis lock acquisition is engineered to Fail-Open:

def acquire_dedup_lock(redis_client, lock_key: str, ttl: int) -> bool:
    if not redis_client:
        return True  # Proceed if Redis is disconnected (Fail-Open)
    try:
        return bool(redis_client.set(lock_key, "1", nx=True, ex=ttl))
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Redis lock check failed: {e}. Failing open.")
        return True  # Guarantee zero message loss during cache failure

During transient Redis latency or network partitions, the system may temporarily allow duplicate enqueues, but business messages safely stored in SQS are never lost.

Answering the Ultimate Skeptic: “Doesn’t Throttling Completely Fail if Redis Dies?”

The candid, unfiltered truth is: yes, if Redis goes down, throttling is temporarily disabled.
Yet the system never fails catastrophically:

  • 1️⃣ Data Integrity Remains Protected: Downstream handlers already enforce business idempotency via idempotency_key, ensuring zero data corruption under duplicate execution.
  • 2️⃣ Zero Message Loss: Instead of rejecting requests (500 Fail-Closed), failing open ensures that customer jobs are never dropped and execute at least once via SQS durability.
  • 3️⃣ Redis is NOT a Single Point of Failure (SPOF): Because Redis acts purely as a “floodgate dam” regulating message volume into MQ rather than an authority on data correctness, a cache outage simply results in temporary over-execution — a textbook implementation of Graceful Degradation.

6. Honest Retrospective: 99%+ Net ROI, Calculated Economic Trade-Offs, and Evolutionary Roadmap

The most debated architectural decision in this system is the synchronous chaining of the Worker Lambda.

In our current implementation, the Worker Lambda pulls from SQS and invokes downstream worker functions (${STAGE}-tj-${job_name}-worker) via RequestResponse, holding an idle socket connection open for 1 to 3 minutes depending on the job:

# worker/lambda_function.py
# 256MB Worker Lambda waits idle while downstream compute executes
response = lambda_client.invoke(
    FunctionName=worker_function_name,
    InvocationType='RequestResponse',
    Payload=json.dumps(job_data)
)

Why Not Asynchronous Invocation (InvocationType='Event')?

Engineers frequently ask: “Why didn’t you invoke the downstream Lambda asynchronously and exit immediately?”
Because the Worker Lambda acts as the enterprise orchestrator. To implement exponential backoff retries (up to 5x), capture full stack traces for Slack failure alerts, and execute sequential pipeline steps (next_jobs), the orchestrator must synchronously capture the downstream execution exit status.

Why Zero Downstream Code Changes? (The Anti-Corruption Layer)

Dozens of existing downstream Lambdas were shared microservices maintained across 10–20 product squads. Forcing all product squads to rewrite their services to support asynchronous message handling would have caused months of roadmapped delays and organizational friction.
Placing the Worker Lambda as an Anti-Corruption Layer (Facade) in front of downstream services delivered distributed throttling with zero downstream code changes — a textbook high-leverage platform decision.

The Economics of Double Billing: 99%+ Net ROI

While synchronous Lambda chaining is officially an AWS anti-pattern, evaluating the financial equation completely changes the perspective:

  • 💸 Lambda Idle Overhead: Running an idle 256MB Worker Lambda for 1 to 3 minutes costs roughly ~0.0003to0.0003to0.0008 USD (less than a tenth of a cent).
  • 💰 LLM Token Savings: Throttling just one redundant LLM call (Claude 3.5 Sonnet / GPT-4o) saves 0.10to0.10to0.50+ USD.
  • 📈 Net ROI Exceeding 99%: Spending less than a tenth of a cent in compute to eliminate dollar-level LLM token waste is an overwhelmingly profitable economic trade-off.

Concurrency Blast Radius & Evolutionary Roadmap

The true risk of synchronous chaining is not cost, but AWS account concurrency pool exhaustion (default 1,000 slots). If hundreds of jobs wait synchronously for 1 to 3 minutes, twice as many concurrency slots are tied up, risking 429 throttling across unrelated, critical APIs.
We mitigated this by configuring Reserved Concurrency on the Worker Lambda and tuning SQS batch concurrency, strictly isolating its blast radius.

  • 🚀 Phase 1 (Current): Worker Lambda Facade for zero-downtime, company-wide rollout and 99%+ net ROI
  • 🚀 Phase 2 (Future Roadmap): Progressively transition downstream workers to AWS Step Functions Express Workflows or direct SQS Event Source Mapping to permanently eliminate idle compute billing

7. Summary & Key Takeaways

  • 1️⃣ Redis for Debouncing, SQS for Durable Execution: Accept Redis volatility, and design cache interactions to fail open so that SQS message durability prevents any message loss during cache downtime.
  • 2️⃣ Plug-and-Play Abstraction via job_name: Build a platform where any AI workload immediately inherits throttling, automated retries, and Slack alerts with zero infrastructure rework.
  • 3️⃣ Atomic Lua Scripts for Window Evaluation & Claiming: Unify cycle resets upon window expiration, remaining delay calculation, permanent lock prevention, and Entry Point Fail-Open into a robust, atomic flow.
  • 4️⃣ Dual-Bucket Partitioning & In-Batch Deduplication: Separate conflicting schedules within a batch into ready_jobs and delayed_jobs, collapsing duplicate bursts into the latest single message to prevent redundant re-queuing.
  • 5️⃣ Reframe Anti-Patterns Through Economic ROI: Do not self-censor pragmatism; spending less than a tenth of a cent to save 0.10–0.10–0.50+ in LLM tokens represents a 99%+ ROI. Pair deliberate technical debt with a clear Step Functions migration roadmap.

item.title: Authentication Mechanisms Every Developer Should Know
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever found authentication confusing? Sessions, JWTs, OAuth, API keys, SSO, passkeys: the list keeps growing, and it’s not always clear which one to use or why.
In this article, we’ll go through the authentication mechanisms the industry relies on today, look at how each one works under the hood and when to use which and their pros and cons.

What is Authentication?

Authentication is how a system checks “Are you really who you say you are?”
Every time a user logs in or a service calls an API, the system needs proof of identity before it can trust the request.
The proof could be a password, a token, a certificate, or a passkey. If it’s valid, the request goes through. If not, it’s rejected with a 401 Unauthorized.

Basic Authentication

This is the most simple authentication mechanism. It involves sending username and password i.e the user credentials with each request to the server.
The server then verifies these credentials before granting access to the requested resource. Though Basic Authentication is easy to understand and implement , but it raises security concerns due to the credentials in plain text.

How it works:

  1. First request: The client asks for a protected resource, such as GET /orders, without any credentials.
  2. Server challenge: The server replies with 401 Unauthorized and a WWW-Authenticate: Basic header. This tells the client it needs to log in using Basic Auth.
  3. Build the credentials: The client joins the username and password with a colon, alice:secret123, and Base64-encodes the result: YWxpY2U6c2VjcmV0MTIz.
  4. Send the header: The client sends the request again, this time with the header:
    Authorization: Basic YWxpY2U6c2VjcmV0MTIz
    This works with any HTTP method: GET, POST, PUT, and so on.
  5. Decode: The server reads the header and decodes the Base64 string to get the username and password back.
  6. Verify: The server checks the username and password against its user store.
  7. Result:
  • Valid: the server returns 200 OK with the requested data.
  • Invalid: the server returns 401 Unauthorized again. The client usually asks the user for credentials again and goes back to step 3.
⚠️ Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone who intercepts the header can decode it in a second. Always use Basic Auth over HTTPS.
When to use it: internal tools, quick prototypes, or simple service-to-service calls over HTTPS.
When to avoid it: public-facing apps. The password goes out with every request, and there’s no built-in logout or expiry.

Digest Authentication

Digest Authentication was designed to fix Basic Auth’s biggest problem: sending the password over the network. With Digest, the password itself is never sent. The client sends a hash that proves it knows the password.

How it works

  1. First request: The client asks for GET /users without any credentials.
  2. Server challenge: The server replies with 401 Unauthorized and a WWW-Authenticate: Digest header. This header contains a nonce: a random value that's valid for a short time only.
  3. Build the hash: The client mixes four things together and hashes them with MD5:
  • the password
  • the nonce from the server
  • a counter (nc), which starts at 1 and goes up with every request
  • the request itself (method + URL, for example GET /users)

4. Retry: The client sends the request again with an Authorization: Digest ... header. It contains the username, the counter and the hash, but not the password.

5. Recompute: The server already knows the user’s password hash. It mixes the same four values and computes the hash on its side.

6. Compare: If both hashes match, the client must know the password.

7. Result: If they match, the server returns 200 OK with the data. If not, it returns 401 Unauthorized.

Why a copied hash can’t be reused

Each hash is tied to one nonce, one counter value and one URL. The server also remembers which counter values it has already accepted.

  • The attacker sends the same request again: that counter value has already been used, so the server rejects it.
  • The attacker raises the counter: the hash no longer matches, and they can’t compute a new one without the password.
  • The attacker tries later: the nonce has expired, so the server rejects it.
Simple example: Alice sends nc=1 with hash X1 and gets in. An attacker copies nc=1, X1, but the server says "counter 1 is already used." The attacker changes it to nc=2, but the correct hash for nc=2 is Y7, and they can't make Y7 without Alice's password.

Why it’s rarely used today

  • MD5 is weak. A captured hash can be cracked offline to recover weak passwords.
  • The server stores password-equivalent hashes. If its database leaks, an attacker can log in as any user.
  • It still needs HTTPS. Without it, an attacker in the middle can tamper with requests.
  • Better options exist. HTTPS combined with token-based authentication solves the same problem more cleanly.

Session-Based Authentication (Cookie-Based)

With Basic Auth, the client sends its password on every request. Session authentication fixes that: the user logs in once, and the server remembers them.

After a successful login, the server creates a session and gives the browser a random session ID. From then on, the browser sends that ID with each request instead of the password.

How It Works

① Login: the session is created

  1. The user sends a username and password to POST /login.
  2. The server checks the password.
  3. If it’s correct, the server creates a session with a random ID, such as sess_8f3k. It saves that ID along with the user's data (userId: 42) in a session store, which can be memory, Redis, or a database.
  4. The server sends the ID back to the browser in a cookie:
    Set-Cookie: SESSION_ID=sess_8f3k; HttpOnly; Secure

② Every request after login

  1. The browser automatically adds the cookie to every request to that site. The frontend doesn’t need any extra code for this.
  2. The server reads the session ID from the cookie and looks it up in the session store.
  3. The store returns who the user is.
  4. The server handles the request for that user.

③ Logout: the session ends

  1. The user logs out.
  2. The server deletes the session from the store.
  3. The server tells the browser to clear the cookie.

A session can also end on its own after a period of inactivity (a session timeout). Either way, the old session ID stops working. If the browser sends it again, the lookup fails and the server returns 401 Unauthorized.

Pros

  • The password is sent only once, at login, not with every request.
  • Easy to revoke: delete the session and the user is logged out immediately.
  • Simple for browsers: cookies are sent automatically.

Cons

  • The server has to store state. Every request needs a lookup, and with multiple servers you need a shared session store like Redis.
  • Session hijacking: if someone steals the session ID, they can act as the user. Use HttpOnly and Secure cookies, and create a new session ID after login.
  • CSRF risk: the browser sends cookies automatically, even on requests triggered by other sites. Use SameSite cookies or CSRF tokens.
  • Not a good fit for mobile apps or APIs. Cookies work best in browsers, and this leads naturally into tokens (JWT), the next section.

API Key Authentication

An API key is a long random string that identifies the calling application. You’ve probably used one already: you sign up for a service, open the dashboard, click “Generate API key”, and paste it into your code.

How it works:

  1. Generate: The service creates a unique key for the client, such as sk_live_9f8a7b2c…, and shows it once.
  2. Send: The client includes the key in every request, usually in a header: X-API-Key: sk_live_9f8a7b2c… or Authorization: Bearer sk_live_9f8a7b2c…
  3. Look up: The server hashes the key and looks it up in its database to find who owns it and what it’s allowed to do(its scopes).
  4. Result:
  • Valid key: 200 OK with the data.
  • Missing, unknown or revoked key: 401 Unauthorized.

API key vs JWT: An API key looks like a token, but it’s just a random string with no information inside it. The server can’t tell who owns it without a database lookup. A JWT carries that information inside the token itself, as we’ll see shortly.

Watch out for:

  • Leaks: anyone who has the key can use it. Never commit keys to Git or put them in frontend code.
  • No built-in expiry: keys live until someone revokes them, so rotate them regularly.
  • Store only a hash of each key, the same way you’d store a password.

Best for: server-to-server calls, public developer APIs, and scripts. Not suited for identifying end users.

Bearer Authentication and JWT

With sessions, the server has to remember every logged-in user. Token-based authentication flips that around: the client carries the proof with it.

Bearer is how you send it, JWT is what you send

A Bearer token simply means “whoever bears (holds) this token gets access.” It’s a way of sending a token in a header:

Authorization: Bearer <token>

It doesn’t say anything about what the token looks like. That’s where JWT (JSON Web Token) comes in. JWT is the most common token format sent as a bearer token.
Inside JWT token:

A JWT has three parts, separated by dots:

  1. Header: the signing algorithm, for example HS256.
  2. Payload: the claims, which are facts about the user such as user ID (sub), role, and expiry time (exp).
  3. Signature: created with a secret key that only the server knows. If anyone changes even one character of the payload, the signature no longer matches.
⚠️ A JWT is signed, not encrypted. Anyone can decode and read the payload, so never put passwords or secrets in it.

How it works

① Login (once)

  1. The client sends its username and password to the Auth Server.
  2. The Auth Server checks them and creates a signed JWT with the user’s claims.
  3. It returns the JWT to the client.

② Every request after login

  1. The client sends the JWT in the Authorization: Bearer header.
  2. The API Server checks the signature and expiry locally, with no database call.
  3. If the token is valid, the server returns the data. A bad signature or expired token gets 401 Unauthorized.

Why this matters

Before JWT, a token was just a random string, like an API key, and every request needed a database lookup. A JWT is self-contained: it carries its own claims and proves they haven’t been changed. This makes it stateless, so any server that has the key can verify it. That’s why it scales so well across microservices.

The trade-off: because the server doesn’t keep any state, you can’t easily revoke a JWT before it expires. If one is stolen, it works until its exp time. The solution is to keep access tokens short-lived, which leads to the next section.

Access Tokens and Refresh Tokens

A short-lived JWT is safer, but nobody wants to log in again every 15 minutes. Modern systems solve this with two tokens:

How it works:

① Login: The user logs in once and gets both tokens.

② Normal use: The client sends the access token with every API request.

③ Access token expires: After 15 minutes, the API returns 401 Unauthorized.

④ Silent refresh: The client sends the refresh token to /refresh and gets a new access token. It then retries the original request. The user never notices.

Why two tokens?

  • If an access token is stolen, it’s only useful for a few minutes.
  • The refresh token is sent much less often, and only to the auth server, so it’s harder to steal.
  • To log a user out, or cut off a stolen device, revoke the refresh token. No new access tokens will be issued.
💡 Store the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie, not localStorage. JavaScript can’t read HttpOnly cookies, which protects the token from XSS attacks. Note that only a server can set an HttpOnly cookie, so this needs a backend to do the token exchange. A single-page app that talks to the auth server directly gets the refresh token in JavaScript, and should rely on refresh token rotation and short lifetimes instead.

OAuth 2: Authorization, Not Authentication

This is the most misunderstood item on the list. OAuth 2 is an authorization framework. It answers:

“What is this app allowed to access on the user’s behalf?”
It does not answer “who is the user?”

Example: a photo-printing app wants to read your Google Drive files. You don’t want to give it your Google password, so you use OAuth 2 to grant limited, revocable access instead.

The four roles:

  • User (resource owner): owns the data
  • Your App (client): wants access to it
  • Google Auth (authorization server): asks the user for consent and issues tokens
  • Drive API (resource server): holds the data

How it works (Authorization Code flow):

  1. The user clicks “Connect Google Drive” in your app.
  2. Your app redirects them to Google, asking for a specific scope, for example drive.readonly.
  3. The user logs in to Google, not your app, and clicks Allow.
  4. Google redirects back to your app with a short-lived authorization code.
  5. Your app’s backend exchanges the code, plus its client secret, for an access token. This happens server to server, so the browser never sees the token.
  6. Google returns the access token.
  7. Your app calls the Drive API with Authorization: Bearer <access token>.
  8. The Drive API returns the user’s files.

The confusing part: at the end, your app has an access token and can read files. It’s easy to think the user has “logged in”. But the access token only proves that the app has permission. It doesn’t reliably tell your app who the user is. For that, you need OpenID Connect.

OpenID Connect (OIDC): Authentication on Top of OAuth 2

OpenID Connect adds an identity layer to OAuth 2. It uses the same redirects, the same code exchange, and the same flow, plus one extra item: an ID token.

This is what runs when you click “Sign in with Google”, “Sign in with GitHub” or “Sign in with Microsoft”.

How it works:

  1. The user clicks “Sign in with Google”.
  2. Your app redirects to Google with scope=openid email profile. The openid scope is what turns this into OIDC.
  3. The user logs in to Google and gives consent.
  4. Google redirects back with an authorization code.
  5. Your app exchanges the code for tokens.
  6. Google returns two tokens:
  • Access token: for calling Google APIs (the OAuth 2 part)
  • ID token: a JWT about the user (the OIDC part)

7. Your app checks the ID token’s signature and reads the claims: sub (a unique user ID), email, name.

8. The user is logged in. Your app usually creates its own session or tokens from here.

OAuth 2 → “This app may read your files.” OIDC → “This is Alice, and Google confirms it.”

That’s why most modern apps use OIDC for login. Your app never handles passwords, and the identity provider takes care of MFA, password resets and account security.

Single Sign-On (SSO) and Identity Protocols

SSO is a user experience, not an authentication method. It means: log in once, and get access to many apps.

You see it every day with Google. Sign in once, then open Gmail, Drive, YouTube and Calendar without logging in again. Companies do the same with Okta or Microsoft Entra ID for Slack, Jira, Salesforce and internal tools.

How it works:

① First app: log in once

  1. The user opens Gmail.
  2. Gmail sees they aren’t logged in and redirects them to the Identity Provider (IdP).
  3. The user enters their credentials. This is the only login screen they’ll see.
  4. The IdP creates a global session and sets an SSO cookie in the browser. It also sends a token proving the user’s identity to Gmail.
  5. The browser opens Gmail again, this time with the token.
  6. Gmail checks the token and shows the inbox.

② Second app: no login screen

  1. The user opens Drive.
  2. Drive also redirects to the IdP.
  3. The browser automatically sends the SSO cookie.
  4. The IdP sees an active session and immediately sends back a token for Drive, without showing a login screen.
  5. The browser opens Drive with that token.
  6. Drive shows the user’s files.

From the user’s point of view, they’re just “already logged in”.

Identity protocols: what SSO runs on

SSO needs a standard way for the IdP to tell an app “this user is Alice”. Two protocols do this:

Both are secure and widely used. New projects should usually choose OIDC. SAML is still common because many enterprises built their systems on it.

Quick Recap

Interview Questions

1. What’s the difference between authentication and authorization? Authentication checks who you are. Authorization decides what you’re allowed to do. Authentication always happens first.

2. When do you return 401 and when do you return 403? 401 Unauthorized means the server doesn’t know who you are: credentials are missing, invalid or expired. 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are, but you don’t have permission.

3. Is Base64 encryption? No. Base64 is encoding, and anyone can reverse it. That’s why Basic Auth is only safe over HTTPS.

Sessions vs Tokens

4. Session-based vs token-based authentication: when would you pick each? Sessions are stateful: the server stores them, and revocation is easy and instant. They’re a good fit for traditional web apps. Tokens (JWT) are stateless: each one carries its own claims, so there’s no lookup and they scale easily across services. They’re a good fit for APIs, mobile apps and microservices.

5. How do you scale session-based auth across multiple servers? Use a shared session store such as Redis, so every server can read every session. The alternative is sticky sessions on the load balancer, but that breaks when a server goes down.

6. What are session hijacking and session fixation, and how do you prevent them? Hijacking: an attacker steals a valid session ID. Fixation: an attacker gets the victim to log in using a session ID the attacker already knows. To prevent both, use HttpOnly and Secure cookies, create a new session ID after login, and set timeouts.

7. What is CSRF, and why do cookies make it possible? Browsers send cookies automatically, even on requests triggered by another site. A malicious page can make the victim’s browser send a request that carries their session cookie. To defend against it, use SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies, CSRF tokens, or tokens sent in the Authorization header instead of cookies.

JWT

8. What’s inside a JWT? Is it encrypted? A JWT has a header, a payload (claims) and a signature. It’s signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read the payload. Never put secrets in it. (JWE is the encrypted variant, but it’s rarely used.)

9. How do you revoke a JWT before it expires? You can’t do it directly, because the server keeps no state. In practice:

  • keep access tokens short-lived and revoke the refresh token;
  • keep a denylist of revoked token IDs (jti) in Redis, which brings back a little state;
  • store a token version per user and bump it to invalidate all of that user’s tokens.

10. HS256 vs RS256: what’s the difference? HS256 uses one shared secret to both sign and verify, so every service that verifies tokens could also create them. RS256 uses a private key to sign and a public key to verify. Only the auth server can issue tokens, while any service can verify them. RS256 is preferred in microservices, often with the public keys published through a JWKS endpoint.

11. What JWT validation mistakes lead to security holes? Accepting alg: none, not checking the signature, ignoring exp, not validating iss and aud, and algorithm confusion (an RS256 public key being accepted as an HS256 secret). Always pin the expected algorithm.

12. Where should you store tokens in the browser? Avoid localStorage, because any XSS script can read it.

  • Browser-only SPA (Authorization Code + PKCE in the browser): the SPA keeps both tokens in memory. The refresh token can’t be HttpOnly, so use refresh token rotation, short lifetimes and, ideally, DPoP to bind tokens to the client.
  • Token-mediating backend: a backend does the code exchange as a confidential client (client secret + PKCE), keeps the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, and gives the SPA a short-lived access token to keep in memory.
  • Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): the backend does the code exchange, keeps all tokens on the server and proxies API calls. The browser only holds a session cookie, so XSS can’t steal any token. This is the option the IETF’s OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications guidance recommends first for sensitive apps.

Access and Refresh Tokens

13. Why use two tokens instead of one long-lived token? To limit the damage if one is stolen. A stolen access token only works for minutes. The refresh token is sent rarely and only to the auth server, and it can be revoked.

14. What is refresh token rotation? Each time a refresh token is used, the server issues a new one and invalidates the old one. If an old refresh token is ever used again, that’s a sign of theft, and the server can revoke the whole token family.

OAuth 2 and OIDC

15. Is OAuth 2 an authentication protocol? No. OAuth 2 is an authorization framework: it gives an app limited access to a user’s resources. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top of it through the ID token.

16. What’s the difference between an access token and an ID token? The access token is for the API: it says what the app may access. The ID token is for the client app: it’s a JWT that says who the user is. Never send an ID token to an API as an access token.

17. Why does OAuth 2 use an authorization code instead of returning the token directly? The code passes through the browser, where it could be exposed. The actual token is fetched server to server using the client secret. Even if someone steals the code, they can’t exchange it without that secret.

18. What is PKCE, and why is it needed? Mobile apps and single-page apps can’t safely keep a client secret. PKCE solves this: the app generates a random code_verifier and sends its hash with the first request. Only the app that knows the original verifier can exchange the code. PKCE is now recommended for all clients.For SPAs, a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) can do the exchange instead of the browser, so no tokens reach JavaScript (see Q12).

19. What are the OAuth 2 grant types, and which ones should you avoid?

  • Authorization Code + PKCE: user login for web, mobile and SPAs.
  • Client Credentials: service-to-service, with no user involved.
  • Device Code: TVs and CLI tools.
  • Avoid Implicit and Password (ROPC). Both are deprecated in OAuth 2.1.

SSO and Design

20. SAML vs OIDC: which would you choose? OIDC for new projects: it uses JSON and JWT, and works well with mobile apps and APIs. Use SAML when you need to integrate with enterprise or legacy systems that already use it.

21. How would you authenticate service-to-service calls in a microservices system? Use the OAuth 2 Client Credentials flow to get short-lived JWTs, or mTLS, where each service proves its identity with a certificate. Many systems use both, often through a service mesh. Avoid long-lived shared API keys.

22. Design an authentication system for a web app and a mobile app.

  • OIDC login, either your own or through an IdP like Auth0, Cognito or Keycloak
  • Authorization Code + PKCE
  • short-lived RS256 access tokens
  • rotating refresh tokens in secure storage
  • JWT verification at the API gateway using JWKS
  • Redis for revocation
  • rate limiting on login
  • MFA
  • HTTPS everywhere
